content:
The
National Statistics Office (NSO), Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), Government of India
, is conducting the
Forward-Looking Survey on Private Corporate Sector CAPEX Investment Intentions (CAPEX 2026)
during the period of
October to
December 2026. The survey is aimed at generating comprehensive and timely information on capital expenditure undertaken and planned by large private corporate sector enterprises, thereby providing important inputs for understanding emerging investment trends in the Indian economy.
1. Objective, Coverage and Method of Data Collection
The primary objective of the CAPEX Survey is to collect information on
capital expenditure undertaken in the recent financial years, provisional capital expenditure in the current financial year and investment intentions for the forthcoming financial year
. The information covers capital expenditure across different asset groups and industries, along with aspects relating to investment strategy, objectives, sources of financing, etc.
The survey covers selected
large private corporate sector enterprises
from different sectors of the economy. The survey frame is prepared using information relating to active enterprises registered with the
Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA)
, subject to prescribed eligibility and turnover criteria. The survey is conducted under the provisions of the
Collection of Statistics Act, 2008
.
Data are collected through a
dedicated and secure web portal
, enabling enterprises to
self-compile and submit
their responses online. The portal provides facilities to assist respondents in understanding the questionnaire, concepts and definitions. The present survey also provides supporting digital resources, including an instruction manual and video guide for portal navigation and self-reporting.
2. Earlier CAPEX Surveys – Key Findings and Outcomes
The National Statistical Office (NSO) conducted the inaugural Forward-Looking Survey on Private Sector CAPEX Investment Intentions (CAPEX 2024) between November 2024 and January 2025.
From this first ever CAPEX survey, the results show that during 2024-25 among the principal activity categories, ‘manufacturing’ accounts for the largest share of aggregate expenditure (43.80%). This is followed by ‘information and communication’ (15.60%) and ‘transportation and storage’ (14.00%).
The detailed results of the CAPEX survey are available in the
CAPEX 2024 Booklet
published by MoSPI:
CAPEX 2024 – Booklet on Findings of the Forward-Looking Survey
The second CAPEX survey was conducted during
October–December 2025
, the findings of this latest CAPEX survey (CAPEX 2025), indicated
that of the provisional aggregate capital expenditure in 2025-26 among
the principal activity categories, ‘manufacturing’ accounts for the largest share of aggregate expenditure (50.17%), amounting to ₹5,73,900 crore. This is followed by ‘information and communication’ (16.38%; ₹1,87,395 crore), ‘electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply’ (8.96%; ₹1,02,448 crore), and ‘transportation and storage’ (5.55%; ₹63,517 crore).
In terms of the proposed scale of CAPEX allocation, nearly 21.16% of enterprises planned to invest more than 80% of their total CAPEX in robotics while the around 78.84% stated that less than 20% of their total CAPEX would be devoted to robotics investments.
As per the estimates obtained from the latest CAPEX 2025 survey (2025-26), the actual CAPEX incurred during 2024-25 by the panel of enterprises was ₹173.5 crore per enterprise, resulting in an overall realisation ratio (RR) of 96.3%, indicating that actual expenditure was broadly in line with the investment intentions at the aggregate level.
From the data collected through the CAPEX survey-2025, the aggregated CAPEX figures (₹ crore) based on data reported by a fixed panel of 3,819 enterprises covering the years 2024-25, 2025-26 and 2026-27 show a modest growth of 1.9% over the actual CAPEX reported by these enterprises in 2024-25. This is given in graph below:
PANEL Estimates on Aggregate CAPEX (in crore)
The detailed results of the CAPEX survey are available in the
CAPEX 2025 Booklet
published by MoSPI:
CAPEX 2025 – Booklet on Findings of the Forward-Looking Survey
3. Launch of CAPEX 2026
Building upon the experience and
outcomes of the earlier two rounds of CAPEX survey, in October 2026, NSO is launching
the
third
CAPEX
survey to
further strengthen the availability of timely information on private corporate investment activity and future investment intentions.
4. Salient Features of CAPEX 2026
The present survey incorporates several features intended to improve the quality, relevance and usability of the information collected as well as to improve the user interface with the portal for submitting information.
Broad coverage of information in the survey:
Collection of information on
past, current and future capital expenditure
Information on CAPEX across
different asset groups and industry sectors
Information on
investment intentions and investment strategies
Investment in
green energy and robotics
Information on the
objectives of investment
, including capacity expansion/upgradation and other investment purposes
Information on
sources of financing
of CAPEX
Features of the web-portal:
Collection through a
secure, dedicated web portal
Facility for
self-compilation and online submission
by enterprises
Digital assistance through an
instruction manual, video guide and AI chatbot
to facilitate portal navigation and reporting
Bilingual
questionnaire
5. Importance of Timely Response
The quality and usefulness of the estimates generated from the CAPEX Survey depend significantly on the
coverage and timely response of the selected enterprises
. Information furnished by individual enterprises contributes to the compilation of aggregate indicators of private corporate investment and helps in understanding the direction and magnitude of investment activity in different sectors.
Timely submission also enables NSO to undertake the necessary validation and processing of the information within the prescribed survey schedule, thereby facilitating the timely availability of reliable statistics for policymakers and other stakeholders.
6. Appeal to the Industry
NSO, MoSPI, therefore,
appeals to all selected private corporate sector enterprises to extend their full cooperation and participate actively in the CAPEX 2026 Survey
. Enterprises are requested to furnish complete, accurate and timely information through the designated web portal.
Enterprises are assured of the confidentiality of their individual data, and that unit-level information will not be disseminated. While
disseminating the survey results, care is taken not to release any information, which could identify the enterprise that has furnished it. While releasing the results, adequate measures are applied to prevent the publication or disclosure of any information deemed confidential. To protect the confidentiality of CAPEX investment plans of individual enterprises, unit-level data of CAPEX survey are not disseminated.
NSO, MoSPI appreciates the cooperation of all selected enterprises in making CAPEX 2026 a successful statistical exercise.

subtitle: Union Sports Minister calls for creation of a comprehensive repository of Physical Education Teachers
ministry: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 3:46PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister for Youth Affairs & Sports Dr. Mansukh Mandaviya today launched the Physical Education Professionals’ Module and highlighted the critical role of PE Teachers in identifying and nurturing sporting talent at the grassroots level.
The Union Sports Minister called for the creation of a comprehensive, nationwide repository of Physical Education (PE) teachers within a time-bound framework to strengthen scientific talent identification and systematic development at the grassroots level.
“Physical education teachers in schools and colleges are among the first to identify sporting talent among children and youth. It is important to map their qualifications, skills and expertise to enable their effective utilisation and further development,” Dr. Mandaviya said after launching the PE Teachers Registration and Onboarding Module on the National Sports Repository System (NSRS).
He further stated, “A nationwide talent identification campaign must adopt a scientific approach, beginning at the grassroots. Many youngsters may possess the right physical attributes and potential to become good athletes with appropriate guidance. Physical education teachers, who spend considerable time with these children, are best placed to identify such talent.”
Outlining the growing importance of Sports Science, Dr. Mandaviya noted that Sports Science has a key role across the sporting pathway, from talent identification and nurturing to the training of elite athletes.
“A scientific approach to talent identification must therefore begin at the grassroots levels,” he added.
Emphasising the need to take the initiative forward in a mission mode, Dr. Mandaviya called for a Physical Education Teachers’ Association campaign at the district level, along with registration and creation of a structured repository at the district, state and national levels.
He said. “Such a repository will help map the capabilities and specialisations of PE teachers and create opportunities for those with special talents to gain exposure at the national and international levels.”
The Union Sports Minister directed that the entire repository should be created within six months and said that its progress would be reviewed in a time bound manner. He said, “The initiative should be taken forward not merely as the launch of a module, but as a mission to develop sports in the country.”
The Physical Education Professionals’ Module has been introduced under the National Sports Repository System (NSRS), a centralised digital platform for maintaining a unified repository of stakeholders associated with the Indian sports ecosystem.
The launch event was attended by senior officials from the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Sports Authority of India (SAI), the Lakshmibai National Institute of Physical Education (LNIPE), the Lakshmibai National College of Physical Education (LNCPE), the Physical Education Foundation of India (PEFI), and other key stakeholders.

title: Shri Rajiv Gauba calls for stronger regulation, market-oriented reforms and institutional capacity to advance India’s energy security and support the vision of Viksit Bharat@2047
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 7:14PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Shri Rajiv Gauba, during his address at the 20th Foundation Day of the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB), highlighted the critical role of regulation, market-oriented reforms and institutional capacity in strengthening India’s energy security and supporting the country’s journey towards Viksit Bharat@2047. He noted that the petroleum and natural gas sector operates in an increasingly complex global environment, marked by geopolitical tensions, supply disruptions, and heightened energy-security risks.
Tracing India's own regulatory journey, he recalled how the sector moved from a colonial-era law and foreign ownership at independence to decades of state control and administered pricing, before progressive liberalisation since the late 1990’s ended the 40-year nomination monopoly and dismantled the administered pricing mechanism. The creation of PNGRB in 2006, he said, was an important institutional step to ensure fair competition, investor confidence and protect consumer interests.
He highlighted PNGRB’s contribution to building the regulatory architecture for natural gas pipelines and noted that its common carrier and contract carrier principles have helped ensure open access to pipeline infrastructure, facilitating greater competition in the downstream market. He emphasised that such regulatory work, while often not visible, is essential for creating predictable markets, building investor confidence and strengthening public trust.
Shri Gauba underlined that India’s growing energy requirements make diversification and expansion of domestic energy capacity important elements of the country’s long-term strategy. With energy demand expected to rise substantially alongside urbanisation, industrialisation and improving living standards, he stressed the need to accelerate domestic exploration and production, particularly in frontier and deep-water activity, while leveraging technology, private investment and the capabilities of public-sector enterprises.
He also emphasised the importance of accelerating India’s transition towards a gas-based economy. This would require an integrated, efficient and economically viable natural gas value chain, including strengthening of the National Gas Grid and improving utilisation of pipelines and LNG terminals, and expanding the City Gas Distribution network.
He noted that regulatory reforms should continue to remove unnecessary frictions and ensure that the regulatory framework keeps pace with emerging areas such as hydrogen, syngas and carbon dioxide pipelines.
Speaking on the future role of PNGRB, Shri Gauba stressed that regulation must evolve alongside technological change and new business models while maintaining primacy of safety and consumer protection. He identified regulatory predictability, ease of doing business and continued reform as important guiding principles for the Board.
He further emphasised that regulatory independence must be accompanied by transparency, reasoned decision-making and accountability. Regulators, he said, have a responsibility to operate at arm’s length while remaining aligned with overarching national policy objectives.

title: PM E-DRIVE Scheme
subtitle: A Step Towards a Sustainable Future
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 7:17PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Electric mobility is gathering pace, driven by targeted policies, financial incentives and supportive measures. At the centre of this shift is the PM E-DRIVE Scheme, launched in September 2024. It aims to accelerate EV adoption, expand charging infrastructure and strengthen the domestic EV manufacturing ecosystem. With an outlay of ₹11,900 crore and implementation extended until March 2028, the scheme supports multiple EV categories and infrastructure. It supports incentives for ~28.30 lakh EVs and has enabled 26.59 lakh sales as of June 2026. The scheme also supports e-buses, charging stations and testing facilities, advancing cleaner, sustainable mobility across India.
India’s Shift Towards Electric Mobility
The country is rapidly transitioning towards electric mobility, with electric vehicle (EV) adoption gaining significant momentum. This is being reinforced through targeted policies, financial incentives and mission-driven initiatives.
At the centre of these efforts is the
PM Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement Scheme (PM E-DRIVE Scheme)
. Implemented from October 2024, it supports faster EV adoption through
upfront purchase incentives
and the
development of charging infrastructure
. By promoting sustainability, the scheme also seeks to
reduce transport-related environmental impacts
and improve air quality.
Breaking Down PM E-DRIVE Scheme
The PM E-DRIVE Scheme is implemented on a pan-India basis.
Originally notified for a two-year period, the Scheme has been extended to
31 March 2028
.
The Scheme has a total outlay of ₹11,900 crore.
It provides
demand incentives
and
infrastructure support
across various vehicle categories and associated components.
The categories covered include
e-2 Wheelers
(e-2Ws),
e-3 Wheelers
(e-3Ws) including registered e-rickshaws & e-carts and L5,
e-Ambulances
,
e-Trucks
,
e-Buses
,
charging infra
, and
upgradation of testing agencies
.
Registered e-2Ws receive an
incentive of ₹2,500/kWh
(capped at ₹5,000 per vehicle). This applies to vehicles priced up to ₹1.5 lakh ex-factory, with a
total fund allocation of ₹2,767 crore
. The scheme aims to support 45.79+ lakh registered e-2Ws.
Target sales for the sub-component registered
e-3W (L5)
have been achieved, and the segment was closed on 26 December 2025.
Support for
e-3Ws
(e-rickshaws and e-carts) continues until March 2028.
Key Achievements of PM E-DRIVE Scheme
PM E-DRIVE supports incentivization of approximately ~28.30 lakh EVs.
26.59 lakh EVs have
been sold
(as of June 2026).
₹4,391 crore has been allocated for the deployment of 14,028 e-buses under PM E-DRIVE. Of these, 14,000 e-buses have been allocated (as of August 2026).
13,800 e-buses
have been allocated to seven cities —
Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Pune and Surat
.
Grant support is also available for
EV public charging stations (EV PCS) and upgradation of testing agencies
.
₹2,000 crore has been earmarked for nationwide EV PCS across India.
₹
851 crore has been approved for deployment of 8147 chargers to 3 oil marketing companies and 10 states (as of 28 September 2026).
₹780 crore has been allocated for modernization and upgradation of vehicle testing agencies.
Impact Across the EV Ecosystem
Government support under PM E-DRIVE is supporting wider EV adoption, cleaner mobility and the development of India’s EV manufacturing ecosystem.
For Buyers
Upfront demand incentives
reduce the purchase price of eligible EVs
, helping lower the initial cost of electric mobility.
E-vouchers enable eligible buyers to receive the demand incentive as an
upfront reduction in the purchase price
, with the amount subsequently reimbursed to the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) by the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
For Cities
The Scheme supports the transition towards
cleaner and more sustainable mobility
through electric buses and other EV categories.
For Industry
PM E-DRIVE supports the development of India’s
domestic EV manufacturing ecosystem
and promotes localisation of EV models.
OEMs registered under the scheme have localised their EV models and obtained
certificates of compliance with the Phased Manufacturing Programme (PMP)
from MHI testing agencies.
The scheme provides
₹780 crore for modernisation and upgradation of vehicle testing agencies
, equipping them with new and emerging technologies
.
Towards a Cleaner Mobility Future
PM E-DRIVE is helping address environmental and energy security challenges while accelerating sustainable mobility. By supporting EV adoption and charging infrastructure, the scheme
strengthens India’s transition towards cleaner and more sustainable transportation
.

title: From First Drop to Clean Streets
subtitle: Cities Prepare for a Cleaner, Healthier Monsoon
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 4:18PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Before the Rains, the Cities Move
As the monsoon approaches and the first rains arrive, cities across India begin preparations to address the seasonal risks associated with waterlogging, waste accumulation, and sanitation. Drains are cleaned, vulnerable locations are identified, and measures are undertaken to maintain cleanliness and public health. Under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs-led
Safai Apnao, Bimaari Bhagao 2025 (SABB)
campaign,
urban local bodies translated pre-monsoon preparedness into a coordinated cleanliness and public health effort. From
1 July to 31 July 2025
, cities undertook drain cleaning, waste removal and hygiene promotion, while engaging communities through schools, neighbourhoods and other public spaces.
At the heart of the campaign are the ‘
6 Swachhata Mantras’:
clean hands, homes, neighbourhoods, toilets, drains and public spaces.
Together, these simple practices are becoming part of a larger city-wide effort to keep the monsoon safer and healthier. And across the country, that effort is taking many different forms.
In
Delhi,
the campaign took the message to its streets and schools. 400 NCC girl cadets led a 3-km
Pinkathon
, a walkathon promoting monsoon hygiene and sanitation.
T
he campaign saw significant on-the-ground action, including handwashing drives in
255 schools
, while
206 cleaning drives
covered backlanes and garbage vulnerable points (GVPs). Another
469 sanitation drives
were conducted in community and public toilets (CTs and PTs).
The Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC) introduced
‘Manhole Ambulances’
to enhance urban safety and sanitation through swift, on-site manhole repairs. Each ambulance carries prefabricated manhole covers, repair tools, and a dedicated response team for immediate action, especially during rains. PMC repurposed old, unused municipal vehicles into functional units. Six ambulances, one per municipal zone, are operational and linked to PMC’s central control room for real-time complaint resolution. The initiative enables citizen-centric grievance redressal and ensures faster responses to manhole-related complaints.
In
Navi Mumbai
,
a Swachhata rally was organised with the participation of over
600
students, parents, teachers, and citizens.
Simultaneously, health awareness camps were held across 26 Urban Primary Health Centres, focusing on malaria and dengue prevention.
Over two days, 52 health camps were conducted, reaching more than 22,690 citizens. In
Telangana
, the campaign reached nearly
13 lakh households
. Around
14,210 km of drains
were desilted, while
4,343 km of roadside bushes
were cleared. Nearly
2.5 lakh houses
were covered through anti-dengue and malaria awareness drives.
Health camps also benefited over
8,500 frontline workers
. Meanwhile,
140 composting pits
were set up in schools, encouraging young citizens to turn waste into manure.
In
Chhattisgarh
, the story begins with people themselves. In
Pandariya
, Self-Help Group members received sanitation training and were introduced to the
Swachhata App
. They then took part in a cleanliness drive. In Raipur, door-to-door outreach promoted hand hygiene and waste segregation, while Garbage Vulnerable Points (GVPs) were cleaned and beautified.
Northeast Unites for a Cleaner, Safer Monsoon
As the monsoon approaches, the Northeast is getting ready not by waiting for the rains, but by preparing for them. Across
Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Assam, Sikkim and Tripura
, the
MoHUA-led SABB campaign
is strengthening monsoon preparedness through collective cleanliness and disease prevention.
In
Nagaland
, Urban local bodies (ULBs) across six towns led school awareness activities, drain cleaning, health camps and cleanup drives. These efforts engaged nearly
5,000 people
through
60 cleanliness, 30 rainwater harvesting and 40 post-monsoon awareness drives
.
Across the hills of
Sikkim
, the campaign took aim at garbage-prone areas and the risks of water- and vector-borne diseases. Students, officials and Self-Help Groups (SHGs) came together around source segregation and better waste management. Around
4,000 people
participated in
100 cleanliness and 100 post-monsoon drives
, alongside awareness rallies and PET bottle shredding initiatives.
In
Assam
, towns focused on drain cleaning, garbage removal, SafaiMitra health check-ups and waste segregation. Around
5,500 people
joined
200 cleanliness and 40 rainwater harvesting activities
, supported by
160 organisations and NGOs
.
In
Tripura
, ULBs strengthened waste collection, segregation and public toilet maintenance. Around
5,000 people
participated in
150 cleanliness and 30 rainwater harvesting drives
, alongside health camps, school rallies and sanitation initiatives.
Across
47 urban notified towns in Arunachal Pradesh
, efforts covered waste management, water quality and public toilet maintenance. Water treatment plants were inspected, while mass cleanliness drives targeted garbage-vulnerable points.
These efforts demonstrate how cleanliness and disease prevention can be integrated into
everyday community action
.
From Backlanes to Clean, Vibrant Neighbourhood Spaces
A
backlane
refers to the space behind houses in a neighbourhood, generally characterised by limited pedestrian movement. Such areas can become vulnerable to waste accumulation and informal dumping. Recognising this, cities across Madhya Pradesh organised
backlane cleaning drives with active public participation
. The initiatives included the removal of encroachments and cleaning of drains to facilitate the smooth flow of rainwater during the monsoon.
In
Rewa
, the Municipal Corporation extended the effort beyond backlanes to improve the cleanliness and appearance of front lanes across all wards. Murals and wall paintings were created, while play equipment and musical instruments were developed using the principles of the
3Rs-Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle
. The walls also feature English and Hindi vowels and alphabets, numbers and multiplication tables. By integrating cleanliness with learning and recreational elements, the initiative has helped create
safer, more engaging and child-friendly neighbourhood spaces
.
In
Agra
, the Agra Municipal Corporation successfully cleaned and maintained
nine backlanes
across the city.
The Urban Learning Internship Program (TULIP) trainees
actively participated in the campaign, while local residents contributed to the cleaning and beautification of neighbourhood streets. Their participation demonstrates how community involvement can strengthen local ownership of cleanliness and support the sustained upkeep of shared public spaces.
From Safety to Opportunity
For
Jyotsna Dhabde of Bhopal
, access to institutional credit provided an opportunity to pursue entrepreneurship. At a Bhopal Municipal Corporation loan fair, she received a loan under the
Swachhta Udyami Yojana
, which enabled her to purchase a sanitation vehicle. In New Delhi,
Raja
, a supervisor with the New Delhi Municipal Council, shared his experience of
mechanised sewer cleaning
.
Raja says, “Earlier, we were compelled to enter the sewers to carry out sewer cleaning. But with the introduction of modern machines, the work is now executed using machines. In addition, being provided with safety gear such as gumboots, masks, safety glasses, helmets, and other protective equipment makes us feel safer.”
Together, these experiences illustrate efforts to make sanitation work safer, more skilled and more dignified.
The
Safai Mitra Suraksha Challenge 2021
focused on health education, the provision and use of safety equipment, worker welfare and reduction of occupational risks. Under
Swachh Bharat Mission–Urban 2.0
, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) has emphasised the provision of protective equipment, training and safety awareness by Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), to work towards
zero fatalities in sanitation work
.
As a pioneer in this space,
Chandigarh
has prohibited hazardous manual sewer cleaning since 2018. An
Emergency Response Sanitation Unit
(ERSU), operating under the
Responsible Sanitation Authority
(RSA), supports safer sanitation practices by providing
Personal Protective Equipment
(PPE), safety gear and regular medical check-ups.
In
Assam
,
83 of 96 Urban Local Bodies (ULBs)
declared themselves
SafaiMitra Surakshit Shehar
in 2023. The state mapped
5,230 sanitation workers
and organised
92 health camps
. In
Maharashtra
,
246 Master Trainers
were prepared during the first phase, followed by training for
1,917 sanitation workers
.
Uttar Pradesh
supported SafaiMitras by facilitating access to credit and livelihood opportunities. Together, these measures seek to strengthen the
safety, social and
economic security, dignity and entrepreneurial opportunities
of SafaiMitras, creating pathways from sanitation work towards
sani-entrepreneurship
.
From Preparedness to Community Action
As the rains arrive, the real value of pre-monsoon preparedness becomes visible on the ground. A cleared drain allows rainwater to flow freely, a clean street prevents waste buildup, and an early health camp helps communities spot and contain disease risks before they spread. At the heart of each measure is the active participation of citizens, making public health a shared responsibility.
From the hills of the Northeast to the streets of Delhi, and across communities in Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh, the campaign has taken diverse, localized forms. Yet underlying them all is a single unified truth:
true monsoon preparedness is not merely about reacting to rainfall, but about preparing together —one street, one neighbourhood, and one community at a time.

title: Finding New Purpose in What We Discard
subtitle: Rethinking Waste from Kitchen Scraps to City Spaces
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 1:40PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM),
launched in 2014, has evolved into a broader movement for cleanliness, waste management, and behavioural change. The mission also created space for wider citizen participation through Swachhata Hi Seva (SHS), launched in 2017 as an annual campaign for collective cleanliness action. The campaign has expanded its focus to plastic waste management, visual cleanliness, and garbage-free public spaces.
Parallelly
,
the idea of
Waste to Wealth
is changing how waste is viewed and managed across India. It treats discarded material as a resource that can be
recovered, reused, and converted
into value. The Government has linked this approach with circularity, resource efficiency, and sustainable waste management. Under Swachh Bharat Mission - Urban 2.0, cities are encouraged to strengthen source segregation, waste processing, and recovery of value from waste. The change is visible not only in large processing plants, but also in homes, communities, and local institutions.
A Compost Bin Brings the Change Home
For many Indian households, turning kitchen waste into compost is not a new idea. It is a practice that is finding a fresh place in today’s waste management systems. In Vijayawada, Andhra Pradesh, senior citizen
K. Subbalakshmi
has shown how this familiar habit can be adopted at home. The municipal corporation recently shared her experience to encourage more citizens to take up home composting. The wet waste generated in her kitchen is converted into compost and used in her garden, returning what would otherwise be discarded to the soil.
A similar effort began in Chandigarh during the COVID-19 pandemic. Resident
Kamaljeet Kaur Deol
started composting wet kitchen waste at home. What began as a household practice gradually grew into awareness activities to encourage others to adopt home composting. Her efforts have since helped inspire citizens to contribute towards a
cleaner and greener city.
As these individual efforts began encouraging wider participation, the idea also found a place in organised community learning. In Siddipet, Telangana, the dedicated waste management learning centre
‘Swachh Badi’
is providing young people with hands-on exposure to practical waste management practices, from home composting to community-level composting. Building on this approach, similar centres are planned across
141 municipal areas
, bringing awareness and practical learning on responsible waste management closer to communities.
What begins with a small compost bin can therefore have a wider effect. It gives new life to plants while keeping a regular stream of wet waste away from landfills. More importantly, it shows how waste management can begin where waste itself is generated.
When a Weed Becomes an Opportunity
Beyond household waste, communities are also finding uses for materials that have long been difficult to manage. In Borchila village of Assam’s Morigaon district, this approach is being applied to a plant that has become a persistent challenge for communities living around water bodies. Water hyacinth, locally known as ‘
pani meteka’
, is an invasive aquatic plant that spreads rapidly across water bodies. Despite its aesthetic appeal, water hyacinth has become a problematic weed, overcrowding freshwater bodies such as rivers, ponds, and lakes. Its overgrowth hampers activities like fishing, transportation, and recreation, making these water sources less viable.
However, the women of Borchila village have found a new way to turn water hyacinth into an opportunity. Instead of viewing the plant only as an unwanted growth in water bodies, they have begun transforming it into handicrafts. Supported under the Assam State Rural Livelihoods Mission, the initiative has created an additional source of income for the participating women, who earn at least
₹10,000 a month
through this work. What was once seen as a problem for water bodies is thus being transformed into a resource for livelihoods and enterprise. The experience demonstrates that resource recovery can extend beyond waste management to create value and livelihood opportunities. By transforming materials that might otherwise remain a burden into useful products, such initiatives can support local enterprise while promoting more sustainable use of resources.
Coconut Waste Finds a New Market
From an invasive plant being transformed into a source of rural livelihood, the focus now shifts to another material contributing to the urban waste burden. In Patna, coconut shells, fibres and other residues are being recovered and processed into useful products. The city generates around
25–30 metric tonnes of coconut shell every day
, which previously added to the volume of waste reaching landfill sites. To address this waste stream, the Patna Municipal Corporation has established a processing facility in the Danapur area, creating a pathway for converting discarded coconut residues into productive resources.
Coconut Waste Processing Plant in Patna
The initiative reflects the systematic approach to waste management promoted under the
Swachh Bharat Mission
, where waste is increasingly viewed as a resource rather than merely a material for disposal. The facility is designed to recover useful components from coconut waste and convert them into products with applications in agriculture, horticulture, and other commercial uses. With an initial processing capacity of
10 tonnes per day
, the plant is planned to operate in multiple shifts and scale up to
30 tonnes per day
.
Ropes made from coconut waste fibers
Different components of coconut waste can be recovered and put to productive use. Wet residues are processed into high-quality organic compost, while coconut fibres are converted into coir ropes with applications in construction, packaging, mats, and handicrafts. Cocopeat is another valuable output, with applications in agriculture and horticulture, including nurseries and rooftop gardens, where its use as a growing medium is gaining importance.
By recovering and processing these materials, the initiative reduces the volume of coconut waste requiring disposal and enables waste-derived products to re-enter productive use. This approach advances circular economy practices while creating avenues for local livelihoods and employment.
When Waste Becomes a Public Space
The idea of Waste to Wealth is also changing how cities look at discarded material. Instead of treating scrap only as waste, cities are finding ways to reuse it in public spaces and community facilities. One such approach is the creation of Waste to Wonder parks, where discarded material is given a new purpose as part of public spaces and attractions. The approach reflects the principles of a circular economy, which encourage materials to be reduced, reused, repaired, and recycled for continued use.
Chandigarh offers an early example of this approach. Its Rock Garden was created using industrial and household waste, demonstrating how discarded material can be creatively reused in a public space. The city has also developed a Waste to Wonder Park spread across 1.75 acres. Structures in the park have been created from discarded materials such as iron sheets, rods, fans, and automobile parts.
Delhi has adopted a similar approach through its
Waste to Wonder Park
, where industrial waste, scrap metal, and discarded automobile parts sourced from landfills are repurposed to create replicas and other structures. Beyond recreation and urban beautification, such spaces demonstrate how discarded materials can be integrated into productive and public-use infrastructure. Beyond urban beautification, the park integrates clean energy infrastructure, featuring solar trees and rooftop solar panels with a combined capacity of 50 KW. The electricity generated can be supplied to power distribution companies, creating an additional avenue for revenue generation while promoting the productive use of waste and renewable energy.
From Waste to Resource
These examples demonstrate how discarded materials can be
recovered, repurposed, and returned to productive use
rather than being sent directly for final disposal. Materials that would otherwise add to the waste burden can be transformed into components of public spaces, creative attractions and, in some cases, sources of economic value.
The
Waste to Wealth
approach begins with a shift in perspective, from viewing waste as something to be discarded to recognising its potential as a resource. Through proper segregation, recovery and processing, discarded materials can be converted into useful products, supporting cleaner communities, resource efficiency and the transition towards a
circular economy
.

title: From AI to EVs: How Technology Is Transforming Urban Swachhata
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 1:01PM by PIB Delhi
content:
On October 2, 2014, the Swachh Bharat Mission began with a simple idea: keep our surroundings clean. Avoid littering public spaces and make cleanliness a shared responsibility. What began with brooms, bins and citizen participation soon became a mass movement. Today, that movement is embracing a new generation of technology.
Urban sanitation is becoming digital, sensor-enabled and electrified.
Digital dashboards are making services easier to track. AI-powered robots are entering spaces too hazardous for workers. Electric vehicles are bringing cleaner mobility to waste collection. From the broom to the bot, technology is giving Swachhata a smarter edge — creating cleaner cities, safer workplaces and more responsive services.
Raipur’s Digital Leap: Dashboard Replaces a Queue
Earlier, Raipur residents had to visit the municipal office for septic tank cleaning services. The new digital system lets residents request desludging services online, reducing the need for an in-person visit and cutting wait times.
Raipur Municipal Corporation has introduced a digital
Faecal Sludge Management (FSM)
dashboard
prototype based on the
UPYOG (Urban Platform for DeliverY of Online Governance) platform.
Residents can use the system to book desludging services, make payments and track the process digitally. The platform is associated with the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA), the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) and the National Urban Digital Mission (NUDM).
The process is designed to be simple. A resident enters a
mobile number or property ID
, and the system automatically locates the address. A single-page form enables desludging to be booked. But the real change happens behind the screen.
Once a request is placed, the system helps track the service in real time. The
“one application, one trip”
approach supports better planning. Drivers upload photographs after completing the work, enabling the service to be verified digitally. The dashboard also helps the city monitor vehicles and plan resources more efficiently.  For sanitation workers, technology is also changing how hazardous work is approached. Digital monitoring supports the shift from manual sewer cleaning towards mechanised cleaning. This reduces human risk and supports safer work practices.
What looks like a simple dashboard is therefore doing more than replacing paperwork. It connects the citizen, the service provider and the municipal system on one digital platform. In Raipur, the journey from “request” to “service” is becoming a trackable digital process.
G-SPIDER: Inside the Canal, a Robot Takes Over
In the heart of Thiruvananthapuram, the
Amayizhanchan Canal
disappears beneath the
Thampanoor railway
premises.  The covered stretch has restricted vertical clearance, continuous water flow and no safe entry points for workers. Conventional cleaning methods therefore become extremely difficult in this confined space.
Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation has brought a robot to clean this difficult space. The city has deployed
G-SPIDER, an AI-powered canal-cleaning system
developed by Technopark-based Genrobotic Innovations, the makers of the robotic scavenger Bandicoot.
The robot uses machine
vision and sensor intelligence
to detect, assess, and remove accumulated waste. It adapts to different waste types, flow conditions and structural challenges in real time. Its
five-degrees-of-freedom mechanism
uses a biomimetic claw to pick up mixed and irregular debris. The extracted waste is then transferred directly into designated collection vehicles.
The significance goes beyond automation. G-SPIDER enhances worker safety by minimising direct exposure to toxic gases, contaminated water and hazardous waste. It can also operate during high water levels and continuous-flow conditions, supporting
scheduled and systematic canal cleaning
.
That makes G-SPIDER more than a cleaning machine. The deployment demonstrates how technology can enable sanitation work in environments where human entry poses significant safety risks. The model also points to wider possibilities. The Thiruvananthapuram deployment showcases a scalable and replicable approach for other high-risk canals and drainage networks.
Garbage Trucks Get an Electric Upgrade
The
daily garbage collection vehicle
is also becoming part of the clean-city transition. Across
Guntur (in Andhra Pradesh), Chennai and Indore cities
, electric vehicles are being integrated into door-to-door waste collection, combining cleaner mobility with smarter waste management.
In Guntur city, more than
200 electric autos
have brought cleaner mobility to door-to-door waste collection across the city. Each
vehicle is equipped with
GPS tracking,
allowing real-time monitoring of collection operations. The initiative eliminates the need for more than
71,000 litres
of diesel annually and is estimated to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by
21,000 tonnes
over a decade.
Tamil Nadu’s Chennai has brought electric mobility directly into its daily waste collection system. The Greater Chennai Corporation has deployed
5,478 battery-operated e-rickshaws
across all 15 zones for door-to-door collection. The vehicles travel around 40 km a day, replacing diesel-powered collection vehicles with e-rickshaws and helping reduce pollution. The fleet reduces around 41 tonnes of carbon emissions each day, amounting to an annual reduction of 15,160 tonnes.
But the change is not limited to cleaner vehicles. Each
e-rickshaw has separate bins for wet, dry and hazardous waste,
bringing segregation into the collection process itself. The fleet now
covers 24,621 streets
and more
than 2.1 million households,
while audio systems on the vehicles carry waste-segregation messages through neighbourhoods. The initiative also supports
employment for more than 6,000 people.
Indore city in Madhya Pradesh has taken the electric transition a step further by linking waste collection with renewable energy. The city has deployed
100 electric vehicles for door-to-door collection
in core areas. Real-time GPS tracking through the Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) supports monitoring and service transparency. The initiative is expected to
reduce annual carbon emissions
by about
24,918 tonnes
and save around
₹5.97 crore
each year in fuel and maintenance costs.
The city has also established
20 solar charging stations
, each equipped with
10 kW solar panels
. Together, they can
generate 800–1,000 units of green energy
daily and
charge 80–100 vehicles
a day.  Across these cities, the garbage collection vehicle is becoming more than a means of transport. It is becoming a cleaner, connected and increasingly efficient part of urban sanitation.
The Next Chapter: Smarter, Safer Swachhata
Technology is giving urban sanitation new tools to clean smarter, work safer and respond faster. From digital dashboards and AI-powered robots to electric waste collection, these innovations are bringing technology closer to everyday Swachhata. The next chapter is about taking these innovations to more cities, adopting them in daily life, making urban sanitation cleaner, safer and more responsive.

title: NHRC, India takes suomotu cognizance of report on 12-member Uttar Pradesh family allegedly kept as bonded labourers for nearly a year at a construction facility in Medchal-Malkajgiri district, Telangana
subtitle:
Reportedly, the rescued bonded labourers lived in hazardous and unsanitary conditions, denied proper wages and subjected to abuse and movement restrictions

The Commission issues notices to the Telangana Chief Secretary, Director General of Police, Medchal-Malkajgiri District Magistrate and Cyberabad Commissioner of Police

Status of 12 rescued victims, investigation, release certificates, financial assistance and long-term rehabilitation plan sought

The Commission directs Medchal-Malkajgiri District Magistrate to take time-bound, victim-centric action
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 7:32PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken suomotu cognizance of a media report regarding a 12-member family from Uttar Pradesh, who were allegedly kept as bonded labourers for nearly a year at a construction facility in Bachupally, Medchal-Malkajgiri district, Hyderabad, Telangana. When rescued, they were reportedly found being paid meagre wages and made to work seven days a week, facing physical and verbal abuse while living in hazardous and unsanitary conditions.
The Commission has observed that the contents of the news report, if true, raise a serious issue of violation of the human rights of the labourers. Therefore, it has issued notices to the Telangana Chief Secretary, Director General of Police, Medchal-Malkajgiri District Magistrate and Cyberabad Commissioner of Police, calling for a detailed report on the matter within four weeks.
The report is expected to include the status and whereabouts of all 12 rescued victims and the steps taken for their immediate safety, shelter, food and medical care. It shall also include details of the FIR registered against the employer and any other responsible persons, along with the status of the investigation. The Commission also directed the Medchal-Malkajgiri District Magistrate to ensure that the entire process of release and rehabilitation is conducted in a time-bound and victim-centric manner.
The report sought from the authorities is also expected to include confirmation of the issuance of Bonded Labour Release Certificates to all eligible victims and provide details of the immediate financial assistance of up to Rs. 30,000 paid to each victim under the Central Sector Scheme for the Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourers, 2021. It shall further include a comprehensive plan for the long-term rehabilitation of the victims, including their repatriation to Uttar Pradesh, if they so desire, in coordination with the authorities in the State.
According to the media report, carried on 30th September 2026, the movement of the bonded labourers was restricted and their belongings were locked away by a supervisor. They were rescued by Revenue and Labour officials following a complaint by social workers.

title: NHRC, India takes suomotu cognizance of the reported incidents of severe chemical burn injuries to workers engaged in 'Bleaching Units' without being provided any protective gear in Panipat district of Haryana
subtitle:
Reportedly, the units are functioning without a valid NOC from the Pollution Control Board

The Commission issues a notice to the Panipat District Magistrate, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 7:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), India has taken
suomotu
cognizance of a media report that a large number of 'Bleaching Units' are operating in Panipat district of Haryana without a valid No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Pollution Control Board. Reportedly, the workers in these units are not being provided boots, gloves or any other safety equipment, due to which they are directly exposed to the hazardous chemical, causing severe damage to their hands and feet apart from skin allergies.
The Commission has observed that the contents of the news report, if true, raise serious issues of violation of human rights. Accordingly, it has issued a notice to the Panipat District Magistrate, calling for a detailed report on the matter within two weeks.
According to the media report, carried on 30th September 2026, due to the use of chemicals like Hydrochloric Acid and Sodium Hypochlorite in these bleaching units, at least 10-12 workers from these units approach the Civil Hospital daily for medical treatment with severely injured hands and feet. Reportedly, no arrangements have been made to dispose the chemical-laden wastewater in these units, which is being directly discharged into pits.

title: Dr. Abhilaksh Likhi, Union Secretary, Department of Fisheries, Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying (MoFAH&D), Chaired Review meeting on National Surveillance Programme for Aquatic Animal Diseases (NSPAAD)
subtitle: Focus on strengthening aquatic animal health, disease surveillance and biosecurity for sustainable aquaculture growth and export-led development of the fisheries sector.
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Fertilizers
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                01 OCT 2026 6:42PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Dr. Abhilaksh Likhi, Union Secretary, Department of Fisheries, MoFAH&D, GoI chaired
review meeting on National Surveillance Programme for Aquatic Animal Diseases (NSPAAD)
on
1st October 2026
in
New Delhi
. The meeting focused on strengthening aquatic animal health surveillance through a review of NSPAAD Phase-I and Phase-II, assessment of the Disease Report App, and discussions on the way forward.
The Review meeting was held through video conference and witnessed participation from State fisheries department, fisheries ICAR institutions including ICAR- National Bureau of Fish Genetic Resources (NBFGR), Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), Export Inspection Council (EIC), Coastal Aquaculture Authority (CAA), National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB) and other relevant fisheries stakeholders.
During the review meeting
, Dr Abhilaksh Likhi
, Secretary (Fisheries), Department of Fisheries, MoFAH&D highlighted the role of NSPAAD program in strengthening disease diagnostics, surveillance networks and laboratory infrastructure to achieve export targets. The Secretary stressed the need for stronger engagement of State Governments, improved convergence among stakeholders and wider adoption of disease reporting mechanisms to enhance disease preparedness and safeguard export competitiveness. He noted that, implemented under PMMSY, the National Surveillance Programme for Aquatic Animal Diseases (NSPAAD) is being executed in two phases to establish a robust aquatic animal disease surveillance and reporting framework in the country. He further suggested examining the transition of NSPAAD from a project-based intervention to a long-term programme under PMMSY to ensure continuity, institutionalization and sustained support for aquatic animal health management in the country. The secretary also sought suggestions from ICAR scientists, state officials to further improve the program outreach.
The stakeholders highlighted the critical role of aquatic animal disease surveillance in sustaining aquaculture growth and supporting India’s expanding seafood exports. Representatives from MPEDA and EIC emphasized the need for closer convergence with NSPAAD to strengthen disease monitoring, ensure compliance with international sanitary requirements and facilitate access to emerging export markets. EIC informed that regular disease reporting and coordinated engagement among regulatory agencies have contributed to easing export certification requirements in key markets such as the Republic of Korea.
ICAR, NFDB, CAA and participating States underscored the need to institutionalize NSPAAD as a long-term programme, strengthen State-level disease surveillance systems and expand farmer participation through the
ReportFishDisease
mobile application. States shared progress in laboratory strengthening, disease diagnostics, awareness generation and farmer outreach, while also highlighting the need for greater adoption of disease reporting tools and enhanced capacity building at the grassroots level. Stakeholders further recommended leveraging Matsya Seva Kendras, Sagar Mitras and fisheries extension networks to improve disease reporting, early warning and rapid response mechanisms across the country.
India’s seafood exports have more than doubled over the past decade, increasing from
₹30,213 crore in FY 2013-14
to
₹73,890.46 crore in FY 2025-26
, reinforcing the country’s position as one of the world’s leading seafood exporters. Recognizing that aquatic animal health is integral to export competitiveness, the Department is simultaneously strengthening disease surveillance, biosecurity and compliance systems to ensure sustainable growth, improved market access and greater acceptance of Indian seafood products in global markets.
The Department is implementing the
National Surveillance Programme for Aquatic Animal Diseases (NSPAAD)
as the country’s flagship aquatic animal disease surveillance initiative. Operational since 2013 and expanded to pan-India coverage under PMMSY since 2022, the programme has established a national network of aquatic animal health laboratories, strengthened diagnostic capacity for WOAH-listed and emerging pathogens, and institutionalised a transparent disease reporting framework aligned with international standards. NSPAAD has conducted over 1,100 awareness programmes covering nearly 48,000 fish farmers and 177 training programmes for stakeholders, while the multilingual
ReportFishDisease
mobile application has enabled timely reporting of disease incidences and rapid scientific response. The programme has facilitated the first-time detection and confirmation of 15 emerging and exotic aquatic animal diseases in the country, strengthened early warning and response mechanisms, and significantly enhanced India’s credibility in international aquatic animal health reporting, thereby supporting the sustainability, resilience and export readiness of the fisheries sector.
